name: Road Cycling
tagline: The peloton's long war — three weeks of Tour, one yellow jersey, endless mountains.
overview: Road cycling races bicycles over public roads in the sport's great formats: one-day classics (Paris-Roubaix's cobbles, Liège-Bastogne-Liège's hills) and the three-week Grand Tours (the Tour de France, Giro d'Italia, and Vuelta a España), where overall champions are decided by seconds across thousands of kilometers. It is the only major endurance sport raced as a team yet won by an individual — the domestique's sacrifice is the genre's defining drama.

The sport's modern structure runs on the UCI WorldTour: nineteen teams of professional riders, the Monument classics' century-old prestige, and the Tour's yellow jersey as sport's most famous garment. Legends define eras — Merckx's five Tours, Hinault's aggression, Induráin's time-trial dominance, and the Armstrong scandal's long shadow that reform-era cycling now lives under — while Tadej Pogačar's era and women's Tour de France (revived 2022) write the current chapters.

Newcomers should start with a road bike fitted properly and group rides: cycling's social structure (clubs, chaingangs, sportives) is the sport's real door. Learn to draft (30% energy savings), climb with rhythm rather than pride, and ride often — the sport rewards accumulated kilometers like almost nothing else.

TT intervals (2×20 min at threshold power); position fitting on the aero bars; cadence and power discipline.

Sprint drills (jump sprints from rolling pace); high-cadence leg speed work; sprint-train practice with teammates.

The free speed: confidence through corners, braking before not during, and the drops' low center of gravity.
Cornering drills in parking lots; descending technique with experienced riders; brake-management practice on known descents.

Reading races: when to pull, when to sit, breakaway math (time gaps, chasing teams' interests), and the peloton's politics.

name: Track Cycling
tagline: Velodrome warfare — banked ovals, fixed gears, and races decided in meters.
overview: Track cycling races fixed-gear, brakeless bicycles on banked oval velodromes (250 m standard, 42° banked corners): sprints of pure power (team sprint, match sprint, keirin) and endurance events of tactical depth (team pursuit, madison, omnium). It has been Olympic since the first modern Games and produces cycling's most explosive athletes — riders who generate 2,000+ watt peaks in events decided by hundredths.

The sport's theater is unique: boxy velodromes with crowds close enough to hear breathing, the match sprint's cat-and-mouse track stand, and the madison's relay chaos. Britain's Olympic factory (Hoy, Kenny, Trott, and the investment era) rewrote the record books through the 2000s-2010s; the Dutch sprint machine and Australia's endurance programs carry the modern rivalry.

Newcomers should find a velodrome's beginner session: track bikes are simpler than road bikes (no brakes, no gears) and the fixed gear teaches pedaling fluency road riding never will. Track racing's entry is genuinely cheap — velodromes lend bikes — and the skills transfer upward into every cycling discipline.

Speed reality

Gear & cadence

Madison sessions with a partner; change timing drills; points-race simulations.

Gym blocks (squats, cleans) in winter; on-track sprint sessions with power measurement; leg-speed work (high cadence, low gear).
rules: Fixed gear, no brakes: the fundamental law — riders slow by resisting the pedals.
Match sprint: best of three heats; the slow-riding phase is legal (track stands included); relegation for forcing opponents up the banking.

Madison: pairs relay with slingshot changes; sprints every 20 laps score points; laps gained subtract 20 points.
Omnium: four events (scratch, tempo, elimination, points) scored cumulatively — track cycling's decathlon.

name: Mountain Biking
tagline: Gravity's playground — rock gardens, singletrack, and the sport born on Marin's slopes.
origin: USA (Marin County) · 1970s klunker era · UCI worlds 1990
overview: Mountain biking races and rides off-road: cross-country (XC) Olympic laps on climbs and singletrack, downhill's gravity-fed runs against the clock, enduro's stage-race format mixing both, and the freeride/trail culture that built the sport's soul. Born when 1970s Marin County riders bombed fire roads on beach-cruiser 'klunkers', it became an Olympic sport (XC, Atlanta 1996) and the most participatory branch of cycling — millions ride trails that exist because mountain bikers built them.

The UCI governs the elite disciplines (world championships since 1990), with Nino Schurter's XC dynasty, Rachel Atherton and Greg Minnaar's downhill eras, and the Enduro World Series defining the competitive map. Beneath the elite runs the sport's real economy: trail associations, bike parks, and a gear industry (full-suspension, dropper posts, tubeless tires) that rewrites itself every few years.

Newcomers should start with a hardtail and local green trails: mountain biking's entry is a skill ladder (body position, braking, cornering) learned by riding, and the community's group-ride culture welcomes every level. Respect trail etiquette (don't skid, yield correctly) and wear the helmet — the sport's one non-negotiable.

Braking drills (emergency stops both wheels); rear-brake slides on gravel (controlled); front-brake confidence circuits.

Corner drills (figure-eights, one-cone circles); berm sessions at a bike park; speed built in increments with the same corner.

Hill repeats on dirt; cadence discipline; strength work (squats, deadlifts) off the bike.

Skills courses and coaching sessions; drop progressions (small to large); rock-garden laps repeated deliberately.

name: Cyclocross
tagline: The mud, the barriers, the beer handups — cycling's off-season festival of suffering.
overview: Cyclocross races road-style bikes with knobby tires over short laps (45-60 minutes elite) of mixed terrain: grass, mud, sand pits, stairs, and the sport's signature wooden barrier sections that force dismount-and-carry. It is cycling's winter sport — October through January, mostly in Flanders' rain — and its atmosphere (music, beer handups, mud-encrusted everything) makes it the most festival-like discipline in bike racing.

Born from Belgian and French road riders racing between villages in winter (the first French championships 1902-era, world championships from 1950), cyclocross built its own religion in Flanders: the Koppenbergcross, Superprestige and World Cup series, and the sport's strange, wonderful ritual where spectators hand riders beer and frites mid-race. The modern era belongs to Mathieu van der Poel and Wout van Aert's rivalry — two generational talents who grew up in 'cross mud and conquered road racing.

Newcomers can start with any bike that takes knobby tires: local 'cross races welcome everyone, and the skills (dismounting, shouldering, remounting, sand riding) are learnable in a season. The sport's entry cost is low, its community warm, and its winter fitness is the secret weapon of every road cyclist who races 'cross.
facts: Founding
Early 1900s France/Belgium — road riders' winter games; first world championships 1950 (Paris)
Governing body

Course format
Laps of 2.5-3.5 km, 45-60 min elite men, 40-50 min women; barriers (4 consecutive), stairs, sand pits, run-ups
The season
October-January: the world championships in late January/early February cap the winter
Equipment
'Cross bikes: drop bars, 33 mm tire max (UCI), disc brakes; road riders race on their road bikes with wider tires
Belgian soul
The sport's heartland: Flanders' 100+ races a winter and the Koppenbergcross's famous hill
history: Octave Lapize-era French riders race cross-country in winter; the first worlds (1950) crown Jean the early champions.
The Belgian golden eras: Eric De Vlaeminck's consecutive titles, Albert Zweifel's Swiss dynasty.

skills: Dismount & remount
The barrier technique: unclip, step through, shoulder the bike, remount at speed without breaking rhythm.
Barrier drills (10 passes per session); remount practice (step-on-the-pedal, not hop); shouldering technique for run-ups.
Running with the bike
The carry: bike on shoulder for stairs and steep run-ups, pushed by the saddle for barriers — efficiency over heroics.
Run-up repeats (find stairs); shouldered-carry intervals; shoe choice and cleat management.
Sand riding
The pit's technique: momentum, low high cadence, weight back, and committed lines.
Sand practice at a beach or pit; line memorization; momentum discipline (slow is sunk).
Cornering in mud
The slide: front-weight management, feathered brakes, and trusting the knob.
Grass corner drills; mud sessions in bad weather (deliberately); tire pressure experiments logged.
Race pacing
45 minutes of intervals with obstacles: red-line efforts between technical sections.
Interval sessions matching race effort; lap-time discipline; rehearsing the start sprint.
Bike handling economy
The total package: mounting, carrying, cornering, and pedaling as one continuous flow — the champions' signature.
Full-course simulations; video comparison with elite lines; flow over speed as the training cue.
rules: Course: laps with marked barriers (four wooden boards), sections run-ups and descents; pits for bike exchanges (equipment changes legal in designated zones).
Duration: elite men 60 min, women 50 min (plus one by rules); juniors and amateurs shorter.

Pits and mechanicals: bike swaps in designated pits; repairs on course allowed with the bike on foot only.

name: BMX Racing
tagline: Eight riders, one hill, forty seconds — the Olympic sprint on two small wheels.
overview: BMX racing sends eight riders down a starting gate onto a 350-450 meter track of jumps, rollers, and bermed turns — a 30-45 second sprint of pedaling, pumping, and positioning won by the front wheel at the line. Born when 1970s California kids imitated motocross on their Sting-Rays, it became an Olympic sport in Beijing 2008 and runs a professional world under the UCI with a world championship every year.

The sport's modern structure: USA BMX's national circuit (the sport's deepest domestic series), the UCI's world cups and worlds, and the Olympic Games' gate. The skills are brutally specific — gate timing, manualing (riding on the back wheel over rollers), and the first-straight battle for the inside line — and the athletes are sprinters: 1,500+ watt efforts with full-body bike control.

Newcomers should start at a local track's beginner day: tracks lend or rent bikes, the learning curve is gate-to-gate fun, and the sport's family culture (it began as a kids' sport and keeps its welcome) makes the entry easy. Learn to pump before you learn to jump: the track's rhythm is the actual skill.

name: BMX Freestyle
tagline: A bike as a paintbrush — parks, streets, and the aerial revolution of two small wheels.
overview: BMX freestyle is cycling as creative expression: riders perform tricks — airs, spins, grinds, and flips — judged on difficulty, execution, and style across disciplines. Park (the Olympic format: concrete bowls and quarter pipes in 60-second runs), street (urban architecture as the playground), vert (the 13-foot halfpipe's big air), flatland (ground choreography on flat concrete), and dirt (trails' jump lines) form the family.

The sport grew from 1980s Southern California (the ramp-and-flatland era of Bob Haro's designs) through the X Games explosion (1995+) and the video-part culture that made riders like Dave Mirra and Ryan Nyquist icons. Olympic park competition arrived at Tokyo 2020 (held 2021), won by Australia's Logan Martin and Great Britain's Charlotte Worthington, and the sport's professional scene now spans contest circuits, video parts, and the Olympics.

Newcomers should expect a skateboard-culture welcome and a long skill arc: learning to bunny hop, then jump, then grind takes months, and every trick has a progression. Ride parks with a helmet, follow session etiquette (drop-in order), and film everything — freestyle's culture is built on clips.

name: Formula 1
tagline: The pinnacle of motorsport — 1,000-horsepower chess at 350 km/h.
overview: Formula 1 is the world championship of open-wheel single-seater racing: twenty drivers in 1,000-horsepower hybrid machines race on circuits from Monaco's harbor walls to Suzuka's figure-eight, across a 24-race global calendar. It is motorsport's technological pinnacle — each team designs and builds its own car within a dense rulebook (the 'formula'), and races are decided by the compound product of driver, machine, strategy, and the pit wall's split-second decisions.

The championship began in 1950 at Silverstone; its lineage runs through Fangio's artistry, Senna-Prost's war, Schumacher's Ferrari dynasty, Hamilton's records, and Verstappen's current era. The sport's modern scale is enormous: 1.5 billion cumulative broadcast viewers, Liberty Media's Drive to Survive-fueled audience boom, and budgets capped at $135 million a season — making F1 simultaneously sport, technology laboratory, and global entertainment product.

Newcomers should watch one full race weekend before judging the sport: qualifying's one-lap drama, the race's strategy layer (tires, pit stops, undercut battles), and the radio traffic between driver and engineer make F1 the most narrated sport on television. The fandom's entry point is free-to-air highlights plus one deep-dive — and the sport rewards obsession like no other.

name: Rallying
tagline: Flat out on gravel, snow, and tarmac — the motorsport of the world's worst roads.
overview: Rallying races production-based cars against the clock on closed public roads: stages of gravel, snow, and tarmac linked by transit sections, with co-drivers reading pace notes that describe every corner before it arrives. The World Rally Championship (since 1973) crowns drivers and manufacturers across a global calendar — Monte's night ice, Finland's flying crests, Kenya's safari dust — and it is motorsport's most complete test: every surface, every weather, every condition.

The sport's lineage runs from the Monte Carlo Rally (1911) through the Group B madness (the 1980s' 500-horsepower fire-breathing era, ended by tragedy), to the modern Rally1 hybrid era. Legends define it: Walter Röhrl's precision, the four multiple Scandinavian titles, Sébastien Loeb's nine, Sébastien Ogier's and the co-driver's art (the notes of Derek Ringer, Julien Ingrassia) as the sport's invisible half.

Newcomers should experience one stage on board (in-car cameras with pace notes are the sport's genius) before watching from outside: rallying's appeal is the co-driver's voice and the sheer commitment on surfaces no circuit would allow. Club rallying exists everywhere — navigational rallies and stage rallies on a local scale are the sport's broad base.

name: MotoGP
tagline: Motorcycles at the physical limit — 365 km/h, 60° of lean, and the bravest show on Earth.

overview: MotoGP is the world championship of prototype motorcycle road racing: 1,000cc prototypes producing 300+ horsepower, ridden at lean angles past 60 degrees and speeds beyond 360 km/h, over a 20-round global calendar. It is motorcycle racing's summit — faster than World Superbike, more specialized than any production-based series — and its heroes (Agostini, Doohan, Rossi, Márquez) are motorcycling's global icons.

The world championship began in 1949 (the FIM's oldest world championship), and the MotoGP era (four-stroke prototypes from 2002) defined the modern age: Rossi's nine titles across classes, Márquez's eight and his recovery saga, and the current era's Ducati dominance. The format weekend — free practice, qualifying, the sprint race (2023 addition), and Sunday's Grand Prix — packs the sport's full drama into three days.

Newcomers should watch one full race at Mugello or Phillip Island before anything else: the sport's appeal is visceral — the lean angles, the overtakes at 300 km/h, the sound — and the lore (the Rossi-Márquez wars, Doohan's five) is the richest in motorsport. Track-day riding and club racing are the fan-to-rider bridge, and the sport's safety revolution (airbags, tracks' run-off) makes its risks more managed than ever.

name: Motocross

overview: Motocross races motorcycles on closed dirt circuits of jumps, whoops (rhythmic bumps), and berms: 30-minute-plus-two-lap motos (the sport's brutal format) with two races per round deciding overall victories. It is the roots of modern off-road motorcycling — the FIM world championship (MXGP) since 1957, the American AMA system, and Supercross (the stadium's indoor sibling) as its spectacular cousin.

The sport's mythology runs through Roger De Coster's five 500cc titles, the American era's dominance (Hannah, Bailey, McGrath's seven supercross the sport's American golden age), and the modern stars: Antonio Cairoli's nine titles, Jeffrey Herlings' speed, and Eli Tomac's longevity. Beneath the elites, motocross is one of motorsport's most participatory sports: local tracks everywhere, family paddocks, and a youth pipeline (50cc bikes at age 5) that feeds everything.

Newcomers should take a beginner day at a track: loaner or rental bikes exist, the learning arc (clutch control, standing position, corner lines) is fast, and the sport's community — part paddock, part family reunion — is famously welcoming. name: Karting
tagline: Motorsport's root system — every world champion started on a kart.
overview: Karting races small open-wheel machines (karts) on sprint circuits: no suspension, no differential, direct steering — the purest driver-development machine in motorsport. Every Formula 1 world champion and most of the world's professional drivers came through karting's ladders, and the sport runs its own world championships under the FIA with classes from age 5 (kid karts) to senior KZ shifter karts reaching 160 km/h.

The sport's genius is accessibility married to depth: rental karting is the world's most popular motorsport participation (business parks and indoor tracks everywhere), while competition karting is a serious technical discipline — chassis tuning, tire management, and race craft at wheel-to-wheel proximity. The FIA Karting World Championship's classes (OK, OK-Junior, KZ) and the national series (SKUSA in the US, the British and Italian championships) form the ladder every racing career climbs.

Newcomers can start the same weekend: rental karting sessions teach the racing line's basics, and club racing with used equipment is motorsport's cheapest serious entry ($3,000-8,000 for a competitive used kart package). The skills — weight management, braking discipline, and wheel-to-wheel confidence — transfer to every form of motorsport above it.
